item.title: ASUS Rolls Out WiFi 8 ROG Rapture GT-BN98 In Canada With 30,000 Mbps And Dual 10 G Ports Ahead Of October Launch
item.description:
The first WiFi 8 router from ASUS has entered the Canadian market, and will soon available worldwide.

ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Series Enters Canada Ahead of Worldwide October Rollout, Bringing WiFi 8's Focus on Reliability, Stability, and Lower Latency

A few months ago, ASUS showcased its first WiFi 8 router called ROG Rapture GT-BN98 at Computex, winning the Computex 2026 award. The same router series is now launching as a retail product. This retail availability marks an early move toward the next generation of wireless networking, as the ROG Rapture GT-BN98 series will now be available in Canada, followed by worldwide distribution in October.

The series brings two models: ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro (BN30000) and the ROG Rapture GT-BN98 (BN25000). Both are quad-band WiFi 8 routers that are built around a 2.6 GHz quad-core processor and feature 2 GB of RAM. ASUS claims that these routers can reach up to 30,000 Mbps of combined wireless throughput. These routers also bring dual 10 G ports and four 2.5 G ports for blazing-fast internet speeds.

That said, WiFi 8's biggest strength doesn't lie in its peak speeds, as it boasts the same maximum bandwidth throughput of 23 Gbps as WiFi 7. The new standard brings superior reliability and is based on the IEEE 802.11bn framework that maintains consistent performance when networks are congested or when the signals are weaker. ASUS's testing indicates that the GT-BN98 can provide noticeable performance improvements even with existing WiFi 7 client devices.

The company highlighted technologies such as UEQM (Unequal Modulation) and NPCA (Non-Primary Channel Access) that are intended to improve connection stability and reduce the effects of interference as compatible WiFi 8 devices become available. WiFi 8 can reportedly deliver 2x higher median throughput, up to 2x wider IoT coverage, lower latency through Multi-AP Coordination, and better performance in crowded wireless environments.

GT-BN98 Pro is particularly an interesting product since it targets gamers with ASUS's networking software. Moreover, ASUS has prepared ZenWiFi BN12, a dedicated WiFi 8 mesh system, which will launch in October, offering 12 streams, up to 129 Gbps of combined throughput, and coverage of up to 7,000 square feet with a two-unit configuration.

Keep in mind that 802.11bn standard is still being finalized and ASUS notes that full benefits of WiFi 8 will require both the router and client device to support the technology.

News Source: ASUS

item.title: EXODUS Q&A: You Can’t Max Your Character in One Playthrough, and Your Final Squad May Differ From Everyone Else’s
item.description:
Following my hour-long playthrough of EXODUS 's Khonsu mission at gamescom 2026 , I had the chance to speak with not one but three of the key developers from Archetype Entertainment : VP and General Manager Chad Robertson , Game Director Chris King , and Lead Writer Drew Karpyshyn . What followed was a wide-ranging conversation covering the studio's seven years of work on their debut IP, the shape of the universe it has built, and a great deal of detail about systems the demo only hinted at.

Some highlights: the studio is a bit over 100 people in Austin , though with several hundred more contributing through development partners worldwide. There will be at least six combat companions , and depending on your choices, the team you finish the game with might not be the same as anyone else's. Romances are open regardless of gender but have to be earned, and juggling more than one may well blow up in your face.

The morality system splits into a Paladin path and an Immortal one, which, according to Archetype, is less about good and evil than about whether humanity should hold on to what makes it human or embrace Celestial evolution. And because Time Dilation means your decisions play out across decades, major choices come with a breakpoint system that previews the possible futures branching off them.

Below is our full conversation with Archetype Entertainment about EXODUS, lightly edited for clarity. As a reminder, the game launches on April 7, 2027 for PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series S|X.

Can we start with the studio? Archetype was founded seven years ago, right before COVID. Did that beginning disrupt things?

Chad Robertson: It's been seven years, and I think we probably anticipated being a little bit sooner to release the game , but COVID definitely... We slowed down hiring a bit and really tried to invest in making sure we had the IP and the world set up right in those early years. Then, once we got used to COVID and things went back to normal, we went through a few pretty good stretches.

Chris King: My favorite memory is that we had two rented offices, and then we moved to this new building. We were there two weeks before we all got sent home for COVID, and we never went back.

Chad Robertson: We used it for about a month. Paid rent on it for about a year.

Are you now mostly working from the office?

Chad Robertson: The nucleus of the team is in Austin, Texas, and we're a bit over 100 people . Most of those folks are based in Austin. And then we lean on several development partners across the country, or across the world, actually. So there are several hundred people who have been contributing to the game.

I know you've been setting up the universe for a long time.

Drew Karpyshyn: We've been building the IP. We started very early with a very small team, three of us and a few other key people. We wanted to focus on making sure we had our core values and the core themes we were going to explore. So, of course, Time Dilation. It's a very big part of our universe, and it's one of the things that helps set us apart . Then we started to build onto that, brought other people in. The Awakened became a very big part of the universe.

As we started to get a handle on what we were building, we started to bring in other people like Peter Hamilton, the novelist, to help us flesh things out and make sure we had a very rich, deep universe we could explore for not just the game we're trying to tell, but the books, the Secret Level episode, and hopefully many other games in the future. And the tabletop game.

Right. I know the handbook is out already. Do you plan to do more on that transmedia front?

Chad Robertson: We're still in contact with Peter. There may be some other stuff that comes . The intention with the IP has always been to make a franchise out of it with as many products as possible. Being part of Wizards of the Coast and Hasbro makes that a lot easier, so we can reach into a bunch of different areas, whether it's the tabletop game, movies and media, toys, or whatever.

When it comes to the novels, was the plan always to make two?

Drew Karpyshyn: I think when you work with somebody like Peter Hamilton, you have to trust him to tell the story he wants to tell . One of the big things we believe in is giving creative freedom as much as we can within the framework of the universe. So we let him decide what story he wanted to tell, and I think he decided pretty early that it was going to be two novels. Once we knew that, we adjusted everything to fit with that era.

Are there going to be any characters from the novels who show up in the game?

Drew Karpyshyn: Not directly, but there are some references and things that carry between the books and the games. The books are set 200 years after. They talk about some of the characters you might meet in the game, but they aren't directly connected. They tell a different story.

That's the great thing about the universe we built: you can tell many, many different stories. They might have references to other things, but they don't necessarily have to tie together. You can still have different parts of the Centauri cluster having their own politics and things going on. Because of Time Dilation , every system is a little bit more isolated. There are still connections, there's trade, there's travel, but because it takes years and years to go between them, the civilizations and societies are more independent, which lets us tell a lot more unique stories in the setting.

Chad Robertson: If you take the time to read, start with the first one. There are some really key parts of the IP that Peter introduces very early with the main character in the book, and then you'll see connections to Jun in similar ways, and to some of the technology and things that are large features of the universe.

One of the most intriguing parts of the universe is the Celestials. Jun is trying to harness Celestial technology to defend humanity against some of the bad Celestial species, but they're not all bad, right? Because one of the companions is a Celestial.

Chris King: You just saw a reveal of some of that in the trailer. The first thing I'd say is that the real reason they're trying to harvest Celestial technology is actually to defeat the Rot , this mysterious force that's destroying the machine that keeps your civilization alive. That's your primary goal.

The thing with the Celestials is that they're so far advanced compared to humans, so far evolved . Think of Jun and humans as being down here, and the Celestials way up there. At the start of the game, they're so far advanced, but by the end of the game, as you power up, they actually take notice of what our envoy is doing. That's kind of what they're set up for. Jun is trying to get this Celestial technology to defeat the Rot.

Speaking of Emrys' recent reveal, you said they're defined by a plural consciousness. How does that play out in terms of dialogue and writing?

Drew Karpyshyn: Emrys is a very interesting companion. I think all our companions are interesting, but Emrys is obviously a Deva Celestial. They have, as you said, a plural consciousness, so they see things in a very different way. They consider themselves more of a collective and refer to themselves in the plural.

They've also been around for many centuries. They knew Orion, who is your father, and they've seen a lot of things . They've seen this slow evolution of humanity, and they have a different perspective than some of the other Celestial factions. So I think it'll be very interesting once we let players encounter Emrys and get to know them. I'd better not reveal too much about the companions.

Do you plan to show all the companions one by one before launch?

Chad Robertson: That's kind of a marketing strategy question, but the intention is to get players to see as many as makes sense before we get there. We've got some coming in the next few months, for sure.

Can you share how many companions can be recruited in EXODUS?

Chris King: Six. That's a tough question, actually. It also depends, because we have different types of companions. We have the companions who go on missions, the combat companions. And then we have some others who technically don't go with you on missions, but for example, we have Cara, the pilot. And then we have some companions who feature very prominently in the story but don't go on missions, with some rare exceptions. It gets a little hard to count. But at least six combat companions.

In the demo, depending on what you choose, your relationship with them goes up or down. Can they decide to leave you?

Drew Karpyshyn: We want to make sure the companions feel realistic, so they have their own goals, their own agendas. They're not always going to agree with you, and they're not always going to agree with each other. That's part of the fun of role-playing with companions, trying to manage these relationships, manage the romances, manage their own conflicts and their conflicts with you.

We definitely want there to be consequences for the choices you make in how you interact with the companions. We're not going to go into specifics, but I think it's safe to say that depending on your choices, the team you finish the game with might not be the same as other players' .

You can bring two into battle at the same time, right?

Chris King: How it typically works is that you bring all your companions on the trip and then you choose who goes into combat with you. Then periodically, as you go through a mission, if you run into one of the way stations — we had it disabled for the demo today — you can actually choose to swap companions . If you find someone's not quite working for the type of enemies or encounters you're running into, you can swap.

Speaking of romance, are there any limitations, or can you potentially romance everyone except for Salt?

Drew Karpyshyn: There's a large number of romances . We're not locking it by gender. The romances are something players will have to pursue, though. They won't fall into your lap, you won't accidentally get a romance. You have to pursue it. And like real-life romance, it's not always easy, it doesn't always go the way you want. You have to earn it.

Depending on which romances you have, a lot of players can try to juggle more than one . That might work. It might blow up in your face, depending who you're with and how you handle it. So romance and relationships are definitely a huge part of the experience, and we put a lot of thought and effort into making those fun and interesting for players.

On the mechanics side, to what extent can you customize a companion's playstyle? Skill trees, that sort of thing?

Chris King: They do have skill trees. We try to design the companions so they have a specific, interesting gameplay role , and then they have a skill tree so you can further customize the things you're most interested in.

Can you respec them?

Chris King: Yes, we have respec on both the player side and for all the companions. There are some limitations on the things we allow you to respec on the player side, specifically with the Oath system, because that ties into some of the major choices you make, but everything else you can respec.

Do companions and the player characters fall into roles like support or damage?

Chris King: That's right. That's what I was getting at when I said each companion has a different gameplay style. For example, in the mission you just played, Suliman is the first mission companion you get, and he's built specifically towards a stealth kit. His abilities, his ultimate, his regular attacks are all themed towards that. So if you love stealth gameplay, that's one of the best companions you can bring with you.

But we have other companions like Elise, with the mech. She's more bombastic. She's got huge missiles and stuff. You could use her in stealth, but that's not her ideal role. She's really for when you're going into combat and blowing things up.

One of the things we say internally is that your team is your loadout . You mix and match the skills, abilities, weapons and upgrades you've got with your companions, and that sets up your loadout going into battle.

Speaking of loadouts, can you swap between them? Say with the player character, between one of two loadouts?

Chris King: Sort of. Any time you go into a mission, we let you pick your companions, and then you can switch your inventory in the pause screen or at way stations and set your loadout. You do have everything available to you in the menu , but it's a bit clunky to get in there, and it's locked out when you're in combat. So ideally, when you start the mission, you're setting yourself up for battle, and then as you proceed through a mission, if you want to course correct a bit, you can.

How important will gear be in EXODUS?

Chris King: It's super important. I don't know if you got to play around with some of this when you played the Khonsu mission, but it gives you a sampling of the different stuff you can do. We have you run into some elite units, harder enemies that you'll periodically encounter. They're really interesting, they have backstories, and some of them drop really interesting items . I won't say too much about that one.

In Khonsu, they do drop some upgrades you can use to upgrade your weapon. There's also a sequence where you run into a vendor who can sell you some new suits. The thinking there is that we want to give players a bunch of stuff to experiment with, and then they can figure out what they like using and custom-tailor their playstyle around it.

Is there a crafting system?

Chris King: We do have crafting. We also have salvage. Every time you go on a mission, you'll collect rare Celestial salvage, and then when you come back to your home city of Persepolis, there are vendors who will trade the salvage for really cool upgrades and items .

Do you have gear rarities? Epic, legendary, that sort of thing?

Chad Robertson: We don't use the same terminology, we try to simplify it a little. But for example, in the Khonsu demo, I don't know if you came across this, you can get the Dragonlance suit , which is a really Exotic crafted suit.

I didn't pay too much attention to loot, because I was trying to finish the story. But I saw you get a lot of scrap. Can you recycle it into something useful?

Chris King: When it comes to the scrap specifically, that's primarily used to craft ammo and resources . What makes the Recycler cool is that it's got this crazy forge in it, so you can use scrap to craft material and make ammo. And then when you go to the waystations periodically through a mission, the waystation machine will craft things like health packs and combat abilities.

Do you have a level cap in EXODUS?

Chris King: Sort of. How would I describe it? I don't know what the number is now, because we just rebalanced it, but yes, we do. You cannot max your character out on a single playthrough, though . You have to make some hard choices about where to spend your points. If you wanted to fully fill out the tree, you'd have to do multiple playthroughs.

Is that through New Game Plus, or just another playthrough?

Chad Robertson: We haven't announced or decided whether we're going to do New Game Plus. Right now, it would just be through a new playthrough. Currently, you can't do a playthrough where you fully fill out the skill tree and max level. I think New Game Plus is something we'd probably want to do later , but we haven't committed to it yet.

Is there going to be a difficulty setting?

Chris King: Yep. We're still debating how many. I'd say we'll probably have at least three or four. The lowest is the narrative mode, so players who are really into the story and maybe aren't as into the combat will have a difficulty setting that allows for that. And then all the way up to, if you love punishing Dark Souls-style play, we have a difficulty level for that too .

Are there going to be a lot of boss fights like the bear?

Chad Robertson: There's a ton . I think that's one of the core parts of the story. Maybe not every mission, but in most missions, there's somebody you're going to encounter who's going to be a challenge for you.

Drew Karpyshyn: This is also a way we try to introduce new elements of the universe. For example, the bear fight lets you see how powerful the Awakened can be, and why they can be such interesting companions or such interesting enemies. It helps flesh out the idea of the Awakened in our universe. As you encounter new worlds and new enemies, we're unfolding things . I think it's safe to say you encounter some Celestial-type enemies, too. We don't want to get too specific, but there are definitely going to be some very interesting aliens. So, through the combat, we also help tell the story of these new elements of the universe as you explore more and become more of a force in Celestial politics. You start to encounter more and more powerful enemies, and then you get these crazier and crazier boss fights.

Chris King: Part of the loop we're trying to reinforce is this: in Khonsu, you eventually earn the Petrify glyph about halfway through. Up to that point, you're running into enemies that are giving you problems, and then you get this new Celestial tool that allows you to deal with them. The War Bear in this mission is the ultimate test of Petrify. It's a way to counter some of the bear's attacks. So we're always trying to add new mechanics like that, layer them on, and then introduce a new enemy that uses it in different ways . That's a recurring loop and theme you'd see across a bunch of the other missions with the bosses.

I noticed the bear was immune to certain damage. So all the boss fights have twists like that?

Chris King: That's exactly right. We're trying to mix it up, and there are pros and cons to which companions you'd bring.

In this mission, you could explore a bit and discover different areas. In the final game, how open will EXODUS be?

Chris King: One thing to point out is that we shortened this mission just for the sake of time. There are actually more areas you can explore and more interesting stuff to find, but we streamlined it to fit the hour slot we had.

In general, though, when you go on missions, we embrace what we call wide linear , or open linear. The mission is linear, but it's got a bunch of nooks and crannies, and if you go off the beaten path, you can find a bunch of interesting stuff. I don't know if you ran into this, but there are a bunch of other Kays you can run into besides 42C.

Drew Karpyshyn: And then, as Chris was saying, that's for the missions. We have the open linear, but then you do return to the hub city, Persepolis, and that's where you'll see a lot of the more open gameplay, a lot of optional content, side quests. That's also where a lot of the choices you made on missions play out. You might see things happening in Persepolis that reflect the choices you made and show you some of the consequences of what you've done .

Chris King: When you go on a mission, you basically have a primary objective you have to do, and there's some side stuff that'll pop up along the way. When you go back to Persepolis, you'll get a list of a bunch of different side quests, or optional companion content, or vendors with new things to buy. It opens up a little bit more when you return.

And of course, time has passed when you go back.

Drew Karpyshyn: We have two different kinds of missions, so not every mission is going to involve Time Dilation. For example, the mission you just played, Khonsu, is a space station orbiting Lidon. There's no time dilation there, because you've stayed within your own system.

When you go on an Exodus, a journey that includes Time Dilation, you leave your system, and obviously, years and years are going to pass before you come back, so there are going to be some pretty significant changes . The way the game works is that before you go on one of these Exodus missions, you want to make sure you have everything in place as far as the right allies and resources for the mission, and you want to make sure everything you're leaving behind is going to be able to sustain itself for years while you're gone. You don't want any nasty surprises when you come back.

So a lot of what you're doing is missions to prepare for an Exodus . You need to plan ahead, set everything up, and make sure you have the right people and the right decisions made so that if something goes wrong while you're gone, they can deal with it. And of course, when you come back, there are always going to be unexpected things you didn't plan for , but you're also going to see the things you did plan, the choices you made, played out over years and years. You'll see this amplification of your choices, and that will be reflected when you come home.

It's also a situation where you need to get your affairs in order before you do it . You don't quite know when you're going to get back or what might happen along the way, so it's a very big moment. We tell you that you need to wrap things up, and there are people who may be asking you for favors, and you may never see them again.

Speaking of choices, if you save the Kays in the demo, it triggers Paladin points. So do you have a Mass Effect-style Paragon and Renegade mechanic, or how does it work?

Drew Karpyshyn: We have a morality system, but it's a little different, a little more nuanced than the typical good and evil. We have the Paladin path and the Immortal path. One of the themes we have is whether you want to push humanity forward by embracing Celestial technology and following the path other civilisations have taken, becoming more Celestial, or whether you want to maintain that core of humanity . That's the Paladin path, where you try to hold on to what makes humans human, and a lot of that is empathy. The Celestials are quite ruthless.

If you embrace Celestial technology and choose the Immortal path, you're going down that branch. So it's not just good and evil, it's more about what future you see for your world, for your characters, for your companions, and for civilization as a whole. Do you want to stay human, or do you want to embrace evolution and become like the other Celestials?

Is there a bar you can actually see that shows how far you've gone?

Chris King: That's right. In the menus, there's a specific screen that breaks down what your Paladin and Immortal levels are, and there's a whole set of upgrades for those as well. One other thing I'd add about the morality system is that the choices aren't just dictated by conversations; they're also affected by the upgrades you purchase . So some of the gameplay choices you make feed back into that as well.

Drew Karpyshyn: Another thing we tried to do is make it so that instead of committing to a path and being stuck on it — a lot of the time you start down a path and you're already committed, and it's very disadvantageous to jump to the other one — we tried to make it a little more flexible, so you can go back and forth and pick and choose certain abilities and skills. You're not locked into Immortal or Paladin . There are benefits to going all the way down each path, but there are also benefits to mixing and matching and taking a bit of both.

Let's say you choose Paladin and then Immortal on the next big choice. Does it cancel out on the bar?

Chris King: The bar is basically your standing, and that's what factors in at the end. But the bars are independent, so no, they don't cancel each other out.

There's one other thing I'd mention. We also have this notion of a breakpoint system . Because of Time Dilation, you're strategically thinking about how your choices will play out over many, many years. One of the things that makes Jun special is that he can foresee a little bit into the future, and there are even upgrades that improve it . So when you got to that final choice, there were two graphics that popped up that previewed some of the things that could potentially happen based on that choice.

That's one of the interesting things with those choices. Major moments have these breakpoints, and it pops up and teases the potential outcomes. Because things are going to play out over so many years, you need a way to think long term.

I could probably stay here all day, but I'll ask a couple more about Jun specifically. I know you can customize Jun's gender, but can you customize the visual look, like hair, face, etc.?

Chris King: Yeah, a little bit. So you can play as a male or a female. And then, when the game actually starts, we take you to a character customization screen. Our goal with that is to give you enough options, but to stay true and authentic to Jun, so you can do things like hair and some facial features . You can do things like makeup. So yeah, we do have an assortment of options you can customize. And then when you play the game, eventually you can do things like the suits we talked about. Those are things that will also change your gameplay and looks. When you're in your hometown of Persepolis, we also have customizable clothes, so you can pick different civilian outfits you can wear. Same thing with the companions.

Do you have a transmogrification feature?

Chad Robertson: No, we don't have that.

Also, I wanted to ask, what is the degree to which you can customize the character of Jun, in terms of his behavior and morale?

Drew Karpyshyn: We are telling the story of Jun, who has a very set sort of background history. We have you starting from a fairly similar place, whether you're a male or a female character. We kind of want to make sure that you understand what the backstory is, what the setup is. We're focused more on the changes that you make as the story progresses through your interactions with the other companions, and the choices you make on missions.

We let you then sort of take the story in the direction you want it to go . But in order to tell a compelling story, we kind of had to have the pieces set up in advance. So, you know, what happened in your history, what happened in your past, so that we can then use those to build out the story as we go forward and let the players then sort of direct it moving forward.

Do you have an estimated kind of average length for an average EXODUS playthrough, let's say for a completionist playthrough?

Chad Robertson: We absolutely do, but we're not ready to talk about it. I think it'll be comparable to other games like this; players will be really satisfied with the game's length . There's certainly a sort of crit path playthrough that would be shorter than more of a completionist path. Chris talked about the wide linear design of a lot of the missions and Persepolis itself. The homeworld or home hub has a ton of optional content players can pursue. So, we're feeling pretty good about the length overall. A funny story with it is actually a few years ago, I think we were a little bit in trepidation maybe about if it was going to be as long as we hoped it was going to be, but as more and more content came in, I think players should look forward to a lot of fun and a lot of hours .

So there's going to be a lot of optional stuff?

Chad Robertson: I think there's plenty. There's a streamlined critical path for players to choose. We certainly hope they'll enjoy some of the optional stuff because some of the best nuggets of lore and like companion and story interactions happen inside. But there's some fun stuff there.

Drew Karpyshyn: And a lot of the optional stuff is based on choices you make. So you open or potentially lock on optional content. So again, for a single playthrough, you won't be able to see everything because the choices you make help dictate what other things can happen down the road . So there's a lot of optional content, side quests, things like that that you will need more than one playthrough if you want to see it all or, you know, talk to your friends to learn about stuff that's a little bit more hidden.

Nice. Thank you for your time.

item.title: Our EXODUS Hands-On Makes the Mass Effect Comparisons Unavoidable, As Archetype’s Debut Game Leans Hard Into Choices and Cover Shooting
item.description:
It's been seven years since former BioWare veteran James Ohlen founded Archetype Entertainment in Austin, Texas, later revealing the studio's debut game as EXODUS .

Ohlen has since left Archetype for personal reasons , but the hype for EXODUS remains high, especially among Mass Effect fans. Not only is the inspiration crystal-clear, but Archetype also hired the acclaimed writer of the original trilogy, Drew Karpyshyn , to create the game's narrative. Besides, the whole studio worked hard on the setting, even going so far as to get Peter F. Hamilton to publish two novels and to prepare a tabletop RPG handbook and other related items for P&P fans .

At last, I was able to go hands-on with the game itself at gamescom 2026, when Archetype Entertainment and publisher Wizards of the Coast (which owns the studio) provided access to an hour-long demo that we also got to capture.

The mission we were sent on was NOT an Exodus ; that is to say, the team did not have to travel light-years to reach a remote location, with all that entails, due to the game's Time Dilation mechanics. Instead, it was a far shorter trip from Lidon to Khonsu , a space station that orbits around Lidon itself, the home planet of protagonist Jun Aslan . The occasion is that the bad guy, Jun's half-sibling Gideon , has seized control of the station and imprisoned the native Kay , a species of Awakened frogs, to do his bidding. Khonsu is also strategically vital, as its shield protects Lidon from meteors and other debris, making it a priority to resolve the situation.

Suliman , the party's Raven contact and an active companion for the missions alongside Elise, has acquired authorization codes for one of the supply docks, allowing us to land quietly on Khonsu. Still, the Ghosts , Khonsu's automated security constructs left behind by the Celestials, quickly attack the party, providing the first taste of combat. I t's here that the Mass Effect comparisons become even more obvious : EXODUS is a third-person, cover-based shooter where the main character Jun also wields certain powers. In this case, it's a gauntlet of Celestials origins that can be equipped with different powers; at the beginning of the demo, it launches a spear-like projectile that deals serious damage to foes.

That's when the demo handed me the first real choice. A wounded Zealot, torn up by Ghosts, begged for a medkit . Suliman objects immediately, arguing that we shouldn't spend resources on an enemy soldier, not even one health pack. The Zealot's story, however, moved me enough to acquiesce. He's from Lioness, he signed up as a kid out of what he thought was (misguided) patriotic duty and a decent career, and he had no idea he'd be sent to force a species he has nothing against into line. He blames the lieutenant, who saw the casualty reports and sent them in anyway. It didn't seem like leaving him to bleed out alone would be the right thing to do . Whether there's any payoff to this choice later remains unclear, given the demo's limited scope.

Shortly after, I met the first Awakened Kay, who was downright hilarious. Naming himself 42C , he's clearly an enthusiastic adolescent who listens to a lot of radio, and that's how he's already familiar with Jun's exploits. He can't tell the party where the Zealot leader is, but he volunteers to help anyway , largely because he wants to watch a fight, and follows the group along through the station's water tubes.

The gauntlet (which also has its uses outside of combat, by the way, such as when you can trigger it to erect pillars that allow Jun to reach previously unaccessible areas) got a new combat power shortly afterward. Jun, thanks to his unique Traveler DNA, is able to interact with Celestial relics and absorb their magic-like properties . Khonsu's Celestial Shrine empowers Jun with the ability to Petrify foes (and things, which can be useful during exploration as well).

This turned out to be extremely handy in the subsequent boss fight with Sergeant Zoeller , one of the toughest minions left by Gideon to protect his stake on Khonsu. Zoeller is extremely resilient in his mech-like armor, but Petrify helps a great deal in the fight, especially if you can properly synergize it with the companions' abilities, such as Elise's Knockdown Missile .

Indeed, there seems to be a great deal of tactical flair to be exploited with the companions. While Elise is entirely focused on firepower (her other active skill is Micro-Missile Barrage), Suliman is fantastic for a stealth-first approach with his Shadowstep skill , which teleports him right behind a target and can kill them outright if they don't have a lot of health. Again, it reminded me of BioWare's Mass Effect or Dragon Age because you take the role of a field commander whose role is not only to dish out damage but also to call the teammates' shots at the right time.

A bit after the boss fight with Zoeller is over, I stumble upon a non-hostile construct that seems to have taken a personality of its own, possibly due to the ambient radiation. The construct tells the party that there's an impregnable armory vault nearby; it can help with access, but wants to be paid 500 Marks (the in-game currency, apparently) for the trouble. Suliman points out that it has no way to actually spend Marks, but the construct is undeterred, presenting yet another choice: pay it, or take it down and get the keycard from its mechanical corpse. I went with the former, and Elise jokingly told Jun he got ripped by a construct. Still, the choice granted my character 25 Paladin points , revealing that there is a Mass Effect-like morality system at play in EXODUS.

Then it was time for an environmental puzzle required to liberate the abrasive Kay engineer 13A, though that gets interrupted by yet another of Gideon's stooges, Sergeant Lusinchi , who was also encased in a mech-like armor and therefore had to be confronted much like Zoeller.

By this point in the demo, I had also acquired some new gear, but I didn't really pay much attention to that. My goal was to finish the demo and confront Gideon's Lieutenant on Khonsu, Naomi , who rigged the beacons with explosives. She doesn't care about the fate of the Kay, or even the fact that damaging Khonsu would leave Lidon at serious risk. She's willing to risk it all, especially to spite Suliman's faction. I try to reason with her, but it doesn't work, and just when she's about to blow up the whole station, Suliman ices her with a pistol headshot.

Needless to say, that doesn't go well with her pal, an Awakened bear named Captain Irina Bruin . This is by far the toughest fight of the demo, especially because she's immune to regular ammunition damage. The best option is to let her charge one of four electrically charged pillars and throw everything at her afterward, companion abilities included.

Eventually, the bear is defeated, and that's when the gamescom 2026 EXODUS demo presented me with the final choice. Surprisingly, Suliman extends an offer from his faction to secure control of the beacons, ensuring the loyalty of all future generations of Kay on the station . This would protect them from any future threats like Gideon, but it also sounds highly hypocritical, and Suliman is aware of that: when I suggest leaving the Kay independent, his personal rapport with Jun actually increases, indicating he wasn't fully onboard with that offer.

All in all, it was a promising first slice at the game . It definitely feels like Mass Effect through and through, which is no bad thing; it's not like we're swimming in these kinds of games, anyway. Its main twist, Time Dilation, cannot really be assessed in a demo environment.

The combat was a lot of fun , if a little easy at times. What worries me more at this point is the technical level of polish , which still has a way to go. As you can see in the video, the frame rate is far from ideal, though I quickly verified from the settings menu that no upscaling was enabled. Between that and pre-launch polish, I'm hoping the final game will run much better. I also hope there will be large enough environments to satisfy the explorer in me, but that's another area that must wait for the final verdict.

EXODUS launches on April 7, 2027 for PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series S|X, so there's not much more time left to wait.

item.title: Stupid Never Dies Channels Suda51 And Grasshopper Style, As Director Sasaki Leans Into Punk-Rock and Zombie Chaos – Interview
item.description:
Following my hands-on session with Stupid Never Dies at gamescom 2026 , I had the opportunity to sit down with Director Eiichiro Sasaki to discuss the game's punk-rock aesthetics, unique combat mechanics, Unreal Engine 5 development, and expected completion time. You can find our full conversation below.

NOTE: The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

Q: How did you come up with the concept for Stupid Never Dies , and how do you feel it compares to similar action RPGs?

A: The core action system itself is relatively standard, but what makes this game unique is that we incorporated a distinct time-limitation mechanic. When creating a new experience, it’s crucial to narrow down what elements to focus on. In our case, we focused entirely on blending fast-paced action with that constant time pressure to bring something completely fresh to players.

Q: Visually and sonically, Stupid Never Dies feels reminiscent of titles from Suda51 and Grasshopper Manufacture. Was that an intentional inspiration, particularly with the music?

A: First of all, regarding the music, I love punk rock. That culture directly inspired how we built this world. The visual art style was heavily influenced by punk rock CD jacket art. The overall graphical approach uses a lot of collage techniques, which stems directly from that aesthetic.

Q: Speaking of that time limit, how did you balance making it feel like a meaningful pressure without completely overwhelming the player?

A: Because Stupid Never Dies is an action RPG, your character parameters grow stronger the more you play. So through standard progression, any player will eventually be able to reach and defeat the final boss within the time limit.

However, if you are highly skilled or master deck combinations, you can hit and defeat the final boss in a significantly shorter time. Our main balancing objective was to ensure that every time someone plays, they feel like they are actively improving. The time limit exists to heighten that feeling of personal mastery.

Q: One peculiar design choice is the complete lack of a lock-on targeting system. What drove that decision, and would you be open to adding it if players request it post-launch?

A: The core design concept of Stupid Never Dies is fighting against pressure coming from multiple directions simultaneously. An enemy might attack from your right, requiring an immediate right punch, before another strikes from your left or behind.

To make it seamless to attack in any direction at a moment's notice, we intentionally opted against a hard lock-on system. The combat system was designed from the ground up around fighting freely across 360 degrees.

Q: Running on Unreal Engine 5, the game feels noticeably smooth and well-optimized. What steps were taken during development to achieve that level of performance?

A: When we started development, Unreal Engine 5 was completely new to our team, so we began from the very early stages of learning the engine's architecture. We worked hard to reach a high-performance standard for this launch, and that technical baseline will allow us to push the engine even further in future projects.

Q: Having previously directed titles like Resident Evil 6 and Resident Evil Outbreak , did you bring any specific lessons from those past zombie experiences into Stupid Never Dies ?

A: I simply love zombies as a concept. There is so much potential in the zombie as a character archetype. Looking back at the history of undead media, zombies went from slow-moving corpses to fast, aggressive threats. There are endless ways to evolve their characteristics. With Davy in Stupid Never Dies , we wanted to explore a completely new, humorous side of what a zombie protagonist can be.

Q: How long can players expect a standard playthrough of Stupid Never Dies to take, and is there post-game content?

A: A standard playthrough takes roughly 20 to 30 hours, depending on individual player skill. On top of the main story, we do have extra content available for players to enjoy after completing the game.

Thank you for your time!

item.title: Sony Doubles Down on its Rockstar Alliance with GTA VI DualSense Controllers, Echoing PlayStation’s History of GTA Timed Exclusives
item.description:
Sony Interactive Entertainment used yesterday's meaty State of Play broadcast to unveil two limited edition DualSense Wireless Controllers themed after Rockstar's GTA VI , with both set to land alongside the game itself on November 19 .

The Black Limited Edition is designed around Vice City after dark, all neon and nightlife. The White Limited Edition takes the opposite style, evoking the city at daybreak with white sand and pastel skies. Both retail for $84.99 , €84.99 , £74.99 , or ¥12,480 , which is a $10 premium over a standard DualSense gamepad.

Both are predictably made in limited quantities and go through PlayStation Direct and participating retailers, though availability might be slightly different between the two , based on Sony's announcement. The White model is described as a global release across both channels, while the Black one is supposed to be a PlayStation Direct exclusive in regions where that service operates, with select retailers covering everywhere else.

In Portugal, players can place their pre-orders at playstation.com/store/hardware .

The DualSense controller's unique features are part of why Sony is touting that GTA VI ' plays best on PS5 '. Back in June, a PlayStation Blog post made that claim and explicitly credited the renowned close partnership between the two companies, leveraging the DualSense controller's haptic feedback and adaptive triggers, the audio piped through the controller speaker, and the Tempest 3D AudioTech as justifications. The store listing also carries the PS5 Pro Enhanced badge, though Sony has not yet detailed what those enhancements actually entail.

A rumor from Polish media suggested that a 60 frames per second mode could be released at some point even on base PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X, and, according to leaker Moore's Law Is Dead , the PS5 Pro version might satisfy the requirements for that badge either with a 40 FPS mode or with a 4K resolution output rather than a 60 FPS option that seems hard to achieve given the level of visuals displayed on the Extended Look .

Anyway, the GTA VI-themed Limited Edition DualSense controllers are only the latest chapter in the partnership between Rockstar/2K and Sony on GTA . Grand Theft Auto III, Vice City, and San Andreas all arrived on PlayStation 2 well before turning up anywhere else, a run of timed exclusivity that did a great deal to define that console generation. Liberty City Stories and Vice City Stories went further and launched as outright PlayStation exclusives on PSP. item.title: NVIDIA Confirms DLSS 5 Support Extends To RTX 40 GPUs, But First Focusing On Model Optimization on RTX 50 Series
item.description:
NVIDIA DLSS 5 is going to be released on older RTX 40 GPUs and will be available once the model is fully tuned on RTX 50 series.

NVIDIA RTX 40 GPUs Will Get DLSS 5 Support As Model Optimization Continues on RTX 50 Series

This week, NVIDIA finally launches its DLSS 5 technology, with NBA 2K27 being the first game to offer support for 3D-Guided Neural Rendering. While the initial support is aimed at RTX 50 GPUs based on the Blackwell architecture, NVIDIA is confirming that they plan to extend support to RTX 40 GPUs too, based on the Ada Lovelace architecture.

DLSS 5 is our most computationally demanding model to date. Since we initially announced it in March, we’ve achieved a 5X performance gain and there’s more to come.

Our current focus is on optimizing performance for the GeForce RTX 50 Series with model updates expected later this fall. Once RTX 50 Series performance is more fully tuned, we plan to work on expanding official support to the GeForce RTX 40 Series .

NVIDIA PR to Wccftech

The announcement means that more gamers will be able to take advantage of game-changing visuals with DLSS 5 as showcased a few days ago. NVIDIA isn't giving us an exact date for DLSS 5 support on RTX 40 GPUs yet, but they have provided an indication of when that will be possible.

You see, NVIDIA's DLSS 5 is their most demanding AI model to date. The original demo was run on dual RTX 5090 graphics cards, but the company managed to improve the model by 50% within two months , managing to run it on just one RTX 5090.

In July, NVIDIA got the DLSS 5 model to improve by almost 2.5x, and finally, in August, the model improved by 5x and is able to run across all RTX 50 graphics cards. NVIDIA explained that the improvement to the DLSS 5 model is a combination of basic hardware, software kernel, and co-design optimizations. The model is smaller, faster, looks more realistic, and offers more control to developers than the initial model that was presented during GTC 2026.

Furthermore, NVIDIA isn't stopping here. The company says its optimizations for DLSS 5 will roll out at a much faster pace, making the model run faster and look even better. It looks like we'll be able to get another update later this year that improves the model and brings faster performance to the table.

We can expect the optimizations in the coming months to improve the model's performance by 7-10x from its initial unveiling. That would result in far less impact on performance than the existing 50-60% hit on average. If the model ends up having a 10-15% impact on performance by the end of this year, that would make it possible for gamers to run it without using MFG modes such as 6x or with "Performance" mode upscaling.

Since RTX 40 GPUs don't have MFG support, they need the model to get fine-tuned before it can become viable for their hardware. And that fine-tuning starts at RTX 50 GPUs, and then leads into RTX 40 GPUs. Given NVIDIA's history with model tuning, we might even see RTX 30 support down the road since GPUs down to the RTX 20 series are already supporting DLSS 5 through unofficial mods . The RTX 40 support is great news, and we can't wait to see Ada Lovelace owners enjoy the DLSS 5 goodness on their cards.

IFA is underway, & AMD announced its return to the keynote stage. The announcement came from AMD's SVP and GM of the Computing and Graphics Group, Jack Huynh, who will be hosting the opening "Era of Personal AI" keynote on 4th of September at 5 AM CT.

Although there are no details on what will be presented during the event, AMD does state that they will share their vision of computing and how "AI transforms the relationship between people and technology and unlocks a new frontier of human imagination, creativity, and possibility."

Since the term "Personal AI" is being used, we expect to see some decent announcements around consumer technologies.

Keynote Details:

AMD is expanding its FSR 4 "Redstone" feature set to several generations of RDNA GPU architectures, but the real fun starts with FSR Diamond , the next major update to the FSR tech. So an insight into that will be interesting.

We don't expect any major CPU/GPU announcements outside of these, but a teaser into the next-generation Zen 6 portfolios will definitely make the keynote a lot more interesting as consumers anxiously wait for proper PC updates, both on desktop and mobile fronts .

item.title: Apple Likely To Face Severe Criticism Over A 10-20% Price Hike For The iPhone 18 Pro, But That’s Because You Haven’t Heard How Much It’s Paying In DRAM Costs
item.description:
Riding the DRAM shortage has got to be one of Apple’s biggest tests, whose majority of revenue relies on increased iPhone sales. The latest estimates mention that the Cupertino firm is expected to raise iPhone 18 Pro costs by 10-20 percent, and while that might cause the company’s loyal customers to start raising pitchforks in protest, wait till they find out how much Apple is paying in DRAM expenses alone.

New report estimates that Apple is paying 400 percent more for DRAM costs for the iPhone 18 Pro this year

For the third quarter of 2026, market research firm TrendForce estimates that memory costs would have ballooned to a 400 percent increase compared to a year ago. While Apple continues to negotiate lower prices, it appears to be an exercise in futility because the major DRAM manufacturers don’t appear to offer any such relief, as their financial goals have drastically changed.

Despite paying a 400 percent premium for LPDDR5X RAM chips, the report mentions that Apple will only introduce a 10-20 percent price hike for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, hinting that the California-based giant has more or less absorbed some of the exorbitant costs that come with purchasing this component in bulk while it’s typically unlike Apple to pass over savings to its customers, knowing full well that the buyer will pay top price to experience flagship features, this time, Apple might not have had a choice.

Apart from introducing the A20 Pro , which is said to be Apple’s first 2nm chipset to be found in an iPhone, the company is having to deal with paying massive sums for LPDDR5X RAM. In a previous leak, it was revealed that the use of the new WMCM (Wafer-Level Multi-Chip Module) packaging enables Apple to utilize the available space for increasing the memory bus width to 96 bits instead of purchasing LPDDR6 RAM. This way, Apple not only gets to boost memory bandwidth but doesn’t have to pay extra for the newer memory standard.

A separate report has mentioned that for Apple to maintain iPhone profits, the iPhone 18 Pro’s base model needs to be $270 more expensive . Whatever the company’s decision happens to be, we’ll find out soon enough during its “Surprise and Shine” event scheduled for September 9.

News Source: TrendForce
